paragraphs: Choosing well-understood technology is not an admission of limited ambition. Familiar tools have documented failure modes and established operational practices. Every unfamiliar component creates learning and maintenance demands, so spend that effort where novelty provides a real product advantage. A task tracker rarely becomes better because its database is the newest database; it becomes better through a useful and reliable user experience.

This is particularly important when building with AI. An assistant can generate a convincing scaffold for a technology you do not understand, leaving you unable to assess the result. Prefer a coherent stack you can inspect and operate over a fashionable collection selected independently in different sessions. New tools remain possible choices, but they should earn their place through requirements and evidence.

sections.heading: Build your distinction; reuse utilities carefully
paragraphs: A utility capability must work but usually does not distinguish your product: sending email, processing payments, hosting files, or handling standard authentication. A strategic capability creates the specific value users choose you for, such as Taskboard's planning workflow or reminder rules. Using established services or proven libraries for utilities can free attention for the product-specific work.

A service also creates dependencies. Examine pricing at expected volume, reliability, data handling, export options, and the effort required to leave. Reliable email delivery involves reputation, bounces, spam policies, and compliance, not just sending a network request. Wrap the provider behind a small interface you control so the rest of the application depends on a stable operation instead of provider-specific details everywhere.

sections.heading: Make choices durable without making them permanent
paragraphs: Write an ADR for each significant technology decision. Include the context, realistic alternatives, choice, costs, limitations, and revisit trigger. Then put the selected stack in the README and AI instructions. Future sessions should extend the agreed system rather than introduce another framework or database because a new prompt did not mention the previous choice.

Review recommendations against current official information before adopting them. An assistant may suggest a retired package, an incompatible major release, or a service already covered by the framework. Require a reason for additions and a migration plan for replacements. Consistency is not stubbornness: when evidence changes, update the decision deliberately and explain how existing code and data will move safely.

sections.heading: Check decisions against a realistic operating month
paragraphs: Estimate ordinary usage rather than comparing only free-tier headlines. Include active users, email volume, storage growth, backups, monitoring, and the time needed to respond to failures. Ask what happens if traffic increases or a provider changes a limit. A slightly more expensive service may still be cheaper overall if it removes operational work you are not equipped to perform.

Before committing heavily to an unfamiliar choice, a small focused experiment can answer the riskiest question. Verify deployment, a required integration, or a representative query rather than building an entire prototype product. Record what the experiment showed and what it did not establish. This gives the decision evidence without turning technology evaluation into an endless side project.

chapters.keyIdea: The right technology is one you can understand, operate, afford, and justify against real requirements.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard pairs a TypeScript React interface with a Python FastAPI backend and relational storage, using PostgreSQL in production and SQLite for local work where appropriate. It relies on proven password hashing and an external transactional email provider rather than inventing those utilities. ADRs and AI instructions preserve the stack and require discussion before adding frameworks or databases.

walkthrough.title: Decide whether to operate your own email system
steps: Classify reliable email delivery as a utility rather than the product’s unique value.
List hidden obligations such as sender reputation, bounces, and compliance.
Compare services at a realistic daily email volume, including privacy and reliability.
Choose a provider behind a small application-owned sending interface.
Record cost estimates, trade-offs, and conditions for revisiting the choice.

mistakes: Copying a famous company’s stack without sharing its requirements or team size.
Ignoring maintenance and learning time in a cost comparison.
Building sensitive utility systems from scratch without the necessary expertise.
aiMistakes: The assistant introduces a second framework: compare the diff with the recorded stack.
It recommends deprecated tooling: verify maintenance status and version-specific documentation.
It adds a service for an existing framework feature: require a gap the service actually fills.
tryIt: Build a weighted comparison of two plausible hosting options.
Classify your application’s capabilities as utility or strategic and explain ambiguous cases.
Write a stack ADR with one disadvantage and one measurable revisit trigger.

check.q: Why does familiarity matter with AI-generated code?
check.a: You need enough understanding to review, debug, and challenge the generated implementation.

check.q: What does choosing boring technology mean?
check.a: Preferring established, understandable tools unless novelty offers a concrete advantage.

check.q: What does a decision matrix prove?
check.a: It makes assumptions and priorities visible; it does not prove one option is universally best.

check.q: What should be checked before choosing a service?
check.a: Expected-scale pricing, reliability, data handling, operational needs, and the difficulty of leaving.

chapters.title: Designing Data and Integrations
chapters.question: How can a repeated click or retried message avoid creating duplicate work or charges?
chapters.summary: Data crossings need explicit ownership and contracts. Design storage, APIs, external integrations, and change strategies so duplicates and partial failures do not quietly damage correctness.

sections.heading: Choose storage from the data’s needs
paragraphs: Start with relationships, queries, and consistency requirements. Users, tasks, and labels form related records and benefit from relational storage, transactions, and ownership filters. Large uploads often belong in object storage while the database holds references and metadata. Temporary recreatable values may suit a cache or key-value store. Full-text search and similarity search address different query needs and should not be confused.

A new application can often begin with one relational database. Adding a search engine, cache, or vector index creates another system to secure, back up, monitor, and keep consistent. Adopt another store because a specific requirement demands it, not because a stack diagram seems incomplete without it. Describe which store is authoritative and which values can be rebuilt from other records.

sections.heading: Assign one owner to each record and rule
paragraphs: An owner is the component responsible for maintaining a kind of data and its invariants, the conditions that must remain true. The tasks module owns task rules; the users module owns accounts; notifications owns reminder preferences and delivery coordination. Other modules request operations through the owner instead of directly editing its tables. This establishes a clear place to fix a rule.

A bounded context is an area within which domain meanings, rules, and ownership are kept coherent. You do not need a complicated framework to benefit from that idea. A simple ownership table can prevent two implementations of overdue logic from disagreeing. Ownership does not mean nobody else can read useful information; it means changes and authoritative decisions follow a defined path.

sections.heading: Write an API contract before clients depend on guesses
paragraphs: An API contract states accepted requests and promised responses. Include endpoint paths and methods, authentication expectations, field names, types, limits, optional values, success statuses, and consistent errors. For creating a task, specify the title limit and whether a missing due date is represented by null. Distinguish a machine-readable error code from the human-facing message. A standard format such as OpenAPI can support documentation, checks, and generated clients.

Large lists need pagination so response sizes remain bounded. Define a limit and a continuation cursor or another deliberate paging method. Versioned paths such as /v1/tasks make room for incompatible future interfaces, but a version prefix alone does not prevent breaking changes within that version. The frontend and backend should share the contract rather than independently guessing what the other side means.

sections.heading: Wrap external services and distrust callbacks
paragraphs: Place provider-specific calls behind an adapter, a small module you control. The rest of the application asks it to send an email or perform another operation without knowing the provider's detailed API. This localises credential use, error translation, and replacement work. It does not remove the provider's outages, but it gives your application one place to handle them consistently.

A webhook is a callback from an external system to your endpoint. Verify its authenticity using the provider's documented signature process before trusting its contents. Expect delayed, duplicate, and out-of-order events. Record a unique event identifier and make processing safe to repeat. Where relevant, recording that identifier and changing business state should occur atomically so a crash cannot leave the deduplication record inconsistent with the actual update.

sections.heading: Make retries safe with idempotency
paragraphs: An operation is idempotent when repeating it produces the same intended effect as performing it once. Reading data is naturally repeatable; creating a task or charging a payment usually needs extra design. An idempotency key identifies one intended operation across retries. The client reuses the key for that operation, and the server recognises it and returns the saved outcome rather than performing the operation again.

The implementation must handle concurrent arrivals, not merely check a list and hope requests arrive sequentially. Scope keys appropriately, store the relevant result, and reject incompatible reuse according to the contract. A new intended operation needs a new key. Disabling a button helps usability but does not replace server-side protection because retries can arise from networks, workers, or callers outside the interface.

sections.heading: Plan partial failure and interface evolution
paragraphs: Suppose saving a task succeeds but sending its notification fails. The database and email provider cannot simply be treated as one reliable action. An outbox records the important database change and the intent to send a message in the same transaction. A worker later sends pending messages and retries failures. Delivery still needs duplicate-aware handling; an outbox does not magically guarantee that an external recipient sees exactly one message.

Avoid holding a database transaction open while waiting for an external service. For changing interfaces, prefer additive changes such as new optional fields. For a breaking rename, add the replacement alongside the old field, migrate callers, and remove the old form only when safe. Public APIs may require a parallel version and a stated transition period. Apply the same care to database schemas that old and new application versions may both use.

sections.heading: Test boundaries under awkward timing
paragraphs: A successful single request is only the beginning of integration testing. Try a duplicate arriving before the first attempt finishes, a timeout after the provider completed its action, and a worker restart after sending but before recording success. These scenarios reveal why checking for duplicates must be coordinated with state changes, and why external effects need provider-aware recovery rather than optimistic assumptions.

Write down what the caller can safely retry and how it learns the final outcome. Include ownership and authentication when storing idempotency results so one account cannot obtain another account’s response by guessing an identifier. State the supported retention period rather than implying protection lasts forever. A boundary contract should explain practical limits as well as the happy path.

chapters.keyIdea: Design each boundary for repeated messages, incomplete outcomes, and gradual change rather than assuming one perfect delivery.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard documents versioned task endpoints and supports an idempotency key when creating a task. Its reminders enter an outbox alongside the recorded reminder decision, and a worker uses one email-provider adapter. Ownership rules keep task semantics from diverging between the interface and notifications.

walkthrough.title: Follow a double submission
steps: Generate a unique key for one intended form submission and reuse it for retries.
On the first request, atomically associate the key with creating the task and its result.
On a concurrent or later repeat, return the original task instead of inserting another.
Verify that a different payload cannot silently reuse the same key.
Document key scope and retention, and test retries plus concurrent requests.

mistakes: Treating a disabled submit button as complete duplicate protection.
Letting several modules update the same data with different rules.
Calling an external service while holding database locks.
aiMistakes: The assistant trusts an unsigned webhook: check provider signature verification before state changes.
It deduplicates only after performing the action: test concurrent requests and crash boundaries.
It renames an API field immediately: require a compatibility and migration plan.
tryIt: Create an ownership table for your main entities and rules.
Write one endpoint contract including errors, pagination where relevant, and retry behaviour.
Describe every outcome if the database succeeds but a provider times out.

check.q: What problem does an idempotency key solve?
check.a: It links retries to one intended operation so the server can avoid repeating its effect.

check.q: What should a webhook handler check?
check.a: Authenticity, whether the event has already been processed, and whether its state transition is valid.

check.q: Why use an outbox?
check.a: It records business changes and delivery intent together so pending external work can be retried.

check.q: How can you safely rename a public API field?
check.a: Introduce the replacement alongside the old form, migrate clients, and retire the old form only through a controlled transition.

chapters.title: Designing for Quality and Future Change
chapters.question: Which design habits keep a working application safe and adaptable as it grows?
chapters.summary: Quality comes from explicit tactics, not from hoping finished code will be good enough. Build in trust checks and privacy, measure performance, track compromises, and recognise when a decision or specialist review deserves more care.

sections.heading: Draw trust boundaries and check crossings
paragraphs: A trust boundary marks where data moves between differently controlled areas, such as the browser and your API or an external webhook and your application. Draw these crossings and ask four questions: what are we designing, what might go wrong, what will we do about it, and how will we check the result? This is a practical introduction to threat modelling rather than a promise to predict every attack.

Validate input, establish identity when needed, and check permission for the specific operation. Apply least privilege: users, services, database accounts, and keys receive only the access their jobs require. Use defence in depth so one missed check does not remove every safeguard. Keep database access behind the intended server path, and send providers only the minimum data needed for their task.

sections.heading: Treat privacy as more than secrecy
paragraphs: Security protects information against inappropriate access and change. Privacy also asks whether you should collect it, how long you should retain it, and whether people understand its use. A securely stored but unnecessary personal profile can still create privacy problems. Minimise collection, logging, and retention. Make a map that includes databases, backups, error trackers, email providers, support tools, and any other destination.

Use invented data when asking an AI assistant to debug a problem. Plan how people can inspect, export, and delete their information, and how expired backups eventually stop retaining it. Explain collection and use in a clear privacy notice. Legal duties vary by location and data type, so seek qualified advice when necessary rather than treating a general checklist as legal compliance.

sections.heading: Connect each quality to a tactic
paragraphs: For performance, begin with queries that match real usage, suitable indexes, pagination, and avoiding one query per list item. Measure user-relevant response times before optimising. For reliability, set timeouts, retry appropriate failures safely, design idempotent operations, and move slow work off request paths when justified. Backups matter only if restoration is possible and tested under the conditions the recovery target describes.

Accessibility benefits from shared semantic components, reliable keyboard paths, visible focus, and suitable contrast from the beginning. Maintainability benefits from coherent modules, tests, current documentation, and consistent conventions. None of these qualities appears automatically because a framework advertises support. Specify how the chosen tactic will be verified through tests, measurements, review, or expert evaluation.

sections.heading: Add caches and queues for a demonstrated need
paragraphs: A cache saves results so they do not need to be recomputed or fetched repeatedly. It can speed repeated expensive work but introduces stale-data and invalidation questions. A background job handles slow work users do not need to watch. A queue smooths bursts and separates accepting work from processing it, but it introduces backlogs, retries, and possible duplicate processing.

Choose these mechanisms after diagnosing a concrete symptom. If task listing is slow because it loads labels with hundreds of individual queries, combine the queries before adding a cache. If a measured burst exceeds processing capacity, a queue may help, provided you monitor delay and failures. Every new moving part should solve an identified problem and come with a plan for its own failure modes.

sections.heading: Track debt and distinguish reversible decisions
paragraphs: Technical debt is the extra future cost created by a compromise or a design that no longer fits. Some debt is deliberate and prudent: ship a limited scheduling approach while documenting its delay and replacement trigger. Some is reckless: ignore design or security without understanding the consequences. Debt can also arise through learning when new evidence reveals a better approach. Record what was compromised, why, and how repayment would work.

Keep a small debt list and repay work in areas that repeatedly slow development. Spend more care on hard-to-reverse choices such as public contracts, database structure, and data ownership. Internal names and layouts are usually easier to revise. Repeated bugs, widespread edits for small features, measured missed targets, or disproved assumptions are signals to reconsider the design through an explicit proposal rather than accidental drift.

sections.heading: Know when general knowledge is not enough
paragraphs: Use specialists when the risks exceed your experience. Payments should normally use a provider's hosted checkout so card details do not pass through your systems; handling them yourself creates serious compliance obligations. Health, financial, children's, and other sensitive data may require data-protection and legal advice before collection. An application holding many people's information or supporting important daily work merits independent security review.

Commercial ownership and licensing questions can require a lawyer. Promised accessibility may require an auditor, and contractual uptime or recovery commitments may need experienced operations help. Seeking advice early can prevent expensive redesign or harm. For a small product, the aim is not maximum architectural sophistication: it is a safe current system with clear boundaries, visible risks, and affordable paths to change.

sections.heading: Make quality work visible in normal changes
paragraphs: Quality plans matter when they influence everyday review. A new endpoint should trigger questions about authorisation, result size, sensitive logging, and retry behaviour. A new form should prompt keyboard and error-message checks. A change to stored personal information should update the retention and deletion map. These are small repeated habits, not a separate quality phase reserved for the end.

Revisit the design when evidence accumulates rather than after one frustrating afternoon. Track recurring incidents, measured targets, and the areas repeatedly touched by changes. An ADR proposing evolution should describe the observed problem, alternatives, migration risks, and expected improvement. This keeps redesign focused on a real constraint while preserving the simplicity that still works elsewhere.

chapters.keyIdea: Build safety and evidence into the design, then evolve it deliberately instead of optimising for imaginary perfection.
chapters.taskboard: Taskboard records trust boundaries, quality tactics, and technical debt alongside its design. It uses ownership checks, bounded task lists, an email outbox, and tested recovery practices. Its reminder interval is an explicit limitation, while unfinished export and account-deletion work must be addressed before public release rather than being presented as complete.

walkthrough.title: Investigate a slow task list before caching it
steps: Measure the list response time under the relevant account size.
Inspect query counts and identify whether labels trigger one query per task.
Change data loading to fetch related labels in a bounded number of queries.
Measure again against the target and run behaviour tests.
Add a cache only if an expensive repeated result remains, with explicit invalidation and privacy rules.

mistakes: Collecting personal data without a purpose or retention plan.
Adding infrastructure before identifying the actual bottleneck.
Taking on compromises without recording their cost and repayment trigger.
aiMistakes: The assistant grants administrator permissions: compare every permission with the actual operation required.
It logs full requests for debugging: inspect logging changes for tokens and personal data.
It calls a risky shortcut temporary without documenting it: require a debt entry and an owner.
tryIt: Draw trust boundaries and list checks at every crossing.
Map all destinations for personal data, including backups and providers.
Write three debt entries and distinguish hard-to-reverse decisions from easy experiments.
Identify one scenario where your project would need specialist advice.

check.q: What is least privilege?
check.a: Giving each identity or component only the permissions needed for its job.

check.q: How does privacy differ from security?
check.a: Privacy also concerns appropriate collection, use, retention, and people’s control, not merely protection from unauthorised access.

check.q: When is a cache justified?
check.a: When measurement shows repeated expensive work that caching can address, with stale-data risks understood.

check.q: What makes debt prudent?
check.a: The compromise is understood, recorded, proportionate to its benefit, and paired with a credible repayment plan.
